summary: Describes a lightweight UDP transfer protocol for IRIS that uses one packet per request and response and can optionally compress the contents. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A quick postcard version of a lookup: one question, one answer, each in a single packet.

questions: what port does iris over udp use
how does iris udp compression work
when should i use iris xpc instead of iris lwz
subtitle: A one-packet-per-question way to query an Internet registry over UDP, with optional compression.

tldr.problem: IRIS registry lookups usually need a full transfer protocol, which is heavy when a client only wants to ask one small question and read one small answer.
tldr.mechanism: IRIS-LWZ puts each request and each response in a single UDP packet, with a small binary descriptor in front of an XML payload that may be compressed with DEFLATE.
tldr.outcome: It suits small public lookups on UDP port 715, but it has no in-band authentication or confidentiality and falls back to IRIS-XPC for anything bigger or more sensitive.

facts.label: Default size if path MTU unknown

today: RFC 4993 is a Proposed Standard and its metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is the definition of IRIS-LWZ, and it points to IRIS-XPC (RFC 4992) for requests that need security or large answers.

sections.title: IRIS-LWZ in One Exchange
sections.content:
The Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) can use several transfer protocols, chosen by the server operator and discovered with S-NAPTR (RFC 3958). This document defines one of them: a UDP transfer protocol that is independent of the registry type it carries. Its binding to IRIS is called IRIS-LWZ, for IRIS Lightweight using Compression.

The message pattern is simple. A client sends a request in one UDP packet and the server answers in one UDP packet. Each packet has two parts: a binary payload descriptor and the request or response transaction payload, which is XML. The XML may be compressed with the DEFLATE algorithm (RFC 1951).
sections.eli5: You send one short note with your question, and the other side sends back one short note with the answer. Nothing more.

sections.title: Packet and Descriptor Format
sections.content:
An IRIS-LWZ packet is a payload descriptor followed by a payload of 0 to n octets. In a request, the descriptor is 6 to 261 octets long. In a response it is always 3 octets. Servers MUST be prepared to accept packets as large as 4000 octets, and clients MUST NOT send packets larger than that.

A request descriptor holds a 1-octet header, a 2-octet transaction ID, a 2-octet maximum response length, a 1-octet authority length and the authority itself (0 to 255 octets). The maximum response length is the total UDP packet size the response should not exceed. If the server cannot fit its answer, it MUST reply with size information instead.

A response descriptor is just the header and the transaction ID. The transaction ID lets the client match answers to questions. Clients SHOULD NOT use sequential values and MUST NOT use 0xFFFF, which is reserved for server use. The server copies the request's ID into the response, except that it uses 0xFFFF (with a descriptor error) when the ID was truncated or was itself 0xFFFF.
sections.eli5: Each note starts with a small label saying who it is for, what number this question has, and how long an answer you can handle. The answer carries the same number so you know which question it belongs to.

sections.title: The Payload Header and Types
sections.content:
The 1-octet payload header is numbered with bit 0 as the most significant. Bits 0 and 1 are the version (V), which is 0 for this document. Bit 2 is the request/response flag (RR): 0 for a request, 1 for a response. Bit 3 is PD, set when the payload is DEFLATE-compressed. Bit 4 is DS, set when the sender supports DEFLATE; if it is 0 in a request, the response MUST NOT be compressed. Bit 5 is reserved and MUST be 0. Bits 6 and 7 are the payload type (PT).

The payload type says what follows the descriptor. 00 is an IRIS XML request or response. 01 is version information: in a request it asks the server for it and the payload is empty, in a response the payload is the version information. 10 is size information and 11 is other information; neither has meaning in a request, and sending one is a descriptor error.
sections.eli5: The first byte is a row of little on/off switches. They say whether this is a question or an answer, whether the text is squished, and what kind of message is inside.

sections.title: Version, Size and Other Information
sections.content:
Three payload types carry XML defined in RFC 4991. Version information uses a <versions> root. Here the <transferProtocol> value is iris.lwz1, and the <application> and <dataModel> values are XML namespace identifiers. Servers SHOULD send it when asked, when the descriptor version is not supported, or when the IRIS XML payload version is not supported.

Size information uses a <size> root, and its octet counts are the total UDP packet length: UDP header, payload descriptor and XML payload.

Other information uses an <other> root whose type attribute names an error. A descriptor-error covers things like an si or oi request, the reserved ID 0xFFFF, a truncated descriptor or non-zero reserved bits. A payload-error means XML that cannot be parsed. A system-error means the server can respond but cannot process the request. An authority-error means the authority is not served here. A no-inflation-support-error means a compressed request reached a server that cannot inflate it.
sections.eli5: When the server cannot just answer, it sends a short note instead: here is how big the answer would be, here is what I speak, or here is what went wrong.

sections.title: When to Use UDP and How to Retry
sections.content:
IRIS-LWZ is meant for cases where UDP is appropriate. A request that needs authentication, confidentiality or other security should use another transfer protocol, and IRIS-XPC (RFC 4992) is RECOMMENDED.

The maximum packet size is 1500 octets if the path MTU is unknown. If it is known, the size MUST NOT exceed the path MTU or 4000 octets. A request that fits is sent uncompressed. If it fits only when compressed, it is sent compressed. Otherwise, or if a request yields a size error, the client switches to another transfer protocol.

For retransmission, a client SHOULD start with a 1 second timeout, double it on each retry, and stop retransmitting once it reaches 60 seconds. Clients using other timeouts MUST have dedicated network resources that ensure fairness. Clients MUST NOT have more than one outstanding request unless they have such resources. If a client plans many requests to the same server in a short time, IRIS-XPC is RECOMMENDED because it would be similarly or more efficient.
sections.eli5: Use the postcard for small, public questions. If your question is too big or secret, use a proper letter instead. If no answer comes, wait a bit, ask again, and wait longer each time.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
The document registers the permanent URI scheme iris.lwz, which identifies an IRIS entity made available using XML over UDP. It registers UDP port 715 under the name IRIS-LWZ, with no broadcast or multicast use. It also registers the S-NAPTR application protocol label iris.lwz. The change controller for the scheme and the label is the IESG.

The text also requires XML to use UTF-8 or UTF-16 only, and no other character encoding.
sections.eli5: It gets an official street number (port 715) and a name so that everyone can find the service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IRIS-LWZ is intended for serving public data and provides no in-band authentication or confidentiality. Applications that need them must use out-of-band mechanisms such as IPsec, or a transfer protocol that provides them, such as IRIS-XPC. Without them, an attacker could alter messages in either direction, which could deny use of an IRIS service or supply false information to users.

Because it runs over UDP, servers can be used in reflection attacks, as other UDP protocols such as DNS can. Operators should apply the same mitigations and follow BCP 38 (RFC 2827). Randomized transaction IDs make it harder for spoofed packets to succeed, though this is not guaranteed to stop an attack.
sections.eli5: Postcards can be read or swapped on the way, so do not put secrets on them. Using a random number for each question makes it harder for a trickster to slip in a fake answer.

fields.name: Header
fields.desc: Version, request/response flag, deflate flags and payload type.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.desc: Matches the response to the request; not sequential, never 0xFFFF.

fields.name: Maximum response length
fields.desc: Largest total UDP packet the server should send back.

fields.name: Authority length
fields.desc: Length of the authority field that follows.

items.label: xml
items.desc: An IRIS-based XML request or response.

items.label: vi
items.desc: Version information; an empty request asks for it.

items.label: oi
items.desc: Other information such as errors; response only.
